title: Spark on Kubernetes: Drivers, Executors, and Why Jobs Die
intro: Spark processes data too big for one machine by splitting it across many. On Kubernetes, a job is one driver pod, which plans the work, and a set of executor pods, which do it. When a job fails, the cause is nearly always in how that split went: memory, or uneven data. Jobs run in the namespace spark; today's job is daily-sessionize.

steps.prompt: Find the driver pods in namespace spark.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
daily-sessionize-a1f9c3-driver    1/1     Running   0          41m
hourly-rollup-7c2b0d-driver       0/1     Error     0          3h
steps.explanation: Today's job has been running 41 minutes; an earlier hourly job ended in Error.
steps.why: Spark labels its pods by role. The driver is the job: if it dies, the job is over, and its log is where the job's own account of what happened lives. A driver in Error with executors long gone is the normal picture of a failed job, since the executors are cleaned up when the driver exits.

steps.prompt: List the executors of the running job.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                              READY   STATUS      RESTARTS   AGE
daily-sessionize-a1f9c3-exec-1    1/1     Running     0          41m
daily-sessionize-a1f9c3-exec-2    1/1     Running     0          41m
daily-sessionize-a1f9c3-exec-3    1/1     Running     0          41m
daily-sessionize-a1f9c3-exec-7    1/1     Running     0          2m
daily-sessionize-a1f9c3-exec-4    0/1     OOMKilled   0          41m
daily-sessionize-a1f9c3-exec-5    0/1     OOMKilled   0          29m
daily-sessionize-a1f9c3-exec-6    0/1     OOMKilled   0          14m
steps.explanation: Three healthy executors and a series of replacements that keep being OOMKilled.
steps.why: Spark replaces a lost executor and retries its tasks, so a job can limp along for a long time while one piece of work kills executor after executor. Executors 4, 5, 6, and now 7 are all the same task being retried. That pattern, most executors fine and one slot dying repeatedly, points at the data, not at the cluster.

steps.prompt: Read the end of the driver's log for the job daily-sessionize-a1f9c3-driver.
steps.fake_output:
WARN TaskSetManager: Lost task 117.2 in stage 4.0 (TID 9120, executor 6): ExecutorLostFailure (executor 6 exited caused by one of the running tasks) Reason: The executor with id 6 was deleted by a user or the framework. Container killed: OOMKilled
INFO DAGScheduler: Resubmitting task 117 in stage 4.0 (attempt 3 of 4)
INFO TaskSetManager: Finished task 118.0 in stage 4.0 in 4.1 s (199/200)
steps.explanation: Task 117 of 200 in stage 4 has killed three executors and is on its last attempt; the other 199 tasks finished in seconds.
steps.why: '199/200' finished in four seconds and one that can't finish at all is data skew: one partition holds vastly more data than the rest. Typically a join or a group-by on a key where one value dominates, a null, or a single enormous customer. All of that key's rows go to one task, which doesn't fit in an executor's memory.

steps.prompt:
One task out of 200 keeps running out of memory. What's the right fix?
  a) Give every executor ten times the memory
  b) Deal with the skew: handle the dominant key separately or salt it, enable adaptive skew handling, or filter out the nulls; more memory only postpones it
  c) Add more executors
  d) Retry more times
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true
spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true      # splits oversized partitions at run time

or in the job: filter user_id IS NOT NULL before the join; treat the one huge key on its own path
steps.hint: More executors don't help when all the work is in one task.
steps.explanation: Fix the distribution of the data, not the size of the machines.
steps.why: Parallelism only helps work that's evenly spread. Adding executors gives 199 idle workers and one that still fails; adding memory works until that key grows again. Adaptive query execution handles many cases automatically. The Spark UI's stage page shows it directly: one task with a far larger input size and duration than the median.

steps.prompt: Open the Spark UI of the running job to look at that stage: forward local port 4040 to the driver pod's port 4040.
steps.explanation: The job's web UI is now at http://localhost:4040.
steps.why: The UI lives in the driver and disappears with it, so for finished jobs you need the event log and a history server, which is worth setting up before you need it. On the stage page, sort tasks by duration or shuffle read size: skew is obvious at a glance. Note also that executor memory on Kubernetes needs overhead beyond the JVM heap, the same lesson as performance-incident-001.
